newsitem.title: HAITI: Haiti's Preval defends economic plan, premier.
newsitem.headline: Haiti's Preval defends economic plan, premier.

text.p: Haitian President Rene Preval has one of the toughest jobs in the Western Hemisphere -- trying to bring economic recovery to a nation where most people make less than $100 a year.

His economic plan, which calls for privatisation of nine state enterprises, is under fire from grassroots organisations and parliamentarians who want his prime minister, Rosny Smarth, to resign. The lower house of parliament, which approved the government's economic recovery plan, is to vote on Wednesday on whether to dismiss Smarth.
Preval, who appealed to deputies on Tuesday to give Smarth a chance, strongly defended his prime minister in an interview with Reuters this week.

"In this country it is so difficult to get anything done quickly because of the weakness of government in general," he said. "That is why it is important to allow an official some time before you judge them."
Preval concedes his job is an arduous one. "When I was elected I knew I had to be ready to work very hard for five years, to be serious," he said. "I'm on a mission."
Preval, who came to power in February last year, described his vision of a better life for Haitians in 2000. "I want better roads, schools, hospitals, telephones, electricity."

His plan would allow for foreign investment in the publicly owned telephone and electricity companies, the flour mill, cement plant, the ports and the airport through management contracts, joint ventures and concessions.

"No one is going to invest in Haiti unless there are phone lines to connect with the Internet, unless there is constant electricity," he said. "The Haitian state doesn't have the capital to provide this, so we need foreign companies to provide the funds and technology."
Even though Preval disapproves of calling it privatisation, his opponents say the scheme amounts to selling out the country.

International financial institutions such as the World Bank and Inter-American Development Bank have pledged hundreds of millions of dollars in loans and grants that hinge on the government's commitment to privatise.

Preval is counting on foreign funding to launch infrastructure and agriculture projects. But, after President Jean-Bertrand Aristide backed off from promises to privatise in 1995, leaving the issue to his successor, international investors are wary the process could fall apart again.

The government has also been criticised for growing insecurity in Haiti, which depends on U.N. troops who still patrol the streets. Preval reiterated he would not request an extension of the U.N. mandate, which expires on July 31.
"We obviously need continuing technical support and training for the police. But I'm not going to request the peacekeeping mission to stay in Haiti," he said.

A new police force was formed by foreign trainers to replace a repressive army after a U.S. invasion in Oct. 1994 ousted a military government and restored Aristide to power. But a crime wave that has left at least 40 people dead in less than a month, including several police officers, has frightened Haitians, especially in the capital.

"People are concerned because there are the kinds of crimes never before experienced in Haiti such as gang wars," Preval said, referring to an escalation in the capital's poorest slum, which he attributed to drug dealing. "But the crime rate here is still lower than in most American or European cities."
